metadata.note: Southern Pacific's East Bay Electric Lines - the 'Big Red Cars' - and their 1938-1941 successor the Interurban Electric Railway. In 1911-1912 SP double-tracked and electrified (1,200 V DC overhead) its steam suburban 'locals' in Oakland, Berkeley and Alameda and built several new lines, to answer the Key System's electric ferry trains. Trains of 72-ft steel cars ran from Thousand Oaks, Albany, Berkeley, downtown Oakland, East Oakland/San Leandro (Dutton Avenue) and Alameda to the Oakland and Alameda ferry piers. Electric service began on the Encinal Avenue line on 1 June 1911. The Harrison Street bridge's removal ended the Webster Street line in December 1923, and the March 1933 SP-Key System agreement ended the California Street, Ellsworth Street and 18th Street lines. From 15 January 1939 the surviving lines ran over the Bay Bridge to the Transbay Terminal in San Francisco; the Alameda lines ended 17 January 1941, Seventh Street in March 1941 and Shattuck/Ninth Street on 25/26 July 1941. Ridership peaked near 22 million a year about 1920 and was 9.9 million in 1939. Ferry-era and bridge-era features are separate because the route west of 16th Street changed completely in 1939 (pier versus flyover and bridge). Steam-era SP/Central Pacific locals over the same streets (from the 1860s-1870s) are NOT drawn: they are real passenger service, but their per-line dates were not sourced well enough here; they are a candidate for a separate commuter_rail feature set. The Fruitvale-Melrose stretch of the Seventh Street line ran on SP's four-tracked main line (main-line trains are in other SP layers). The Encinal Avenue line ran over the former South Pacific Coast route on Alameda island and the Lincoln Avenue line over the former San Francisco and Alameda Railroad - both drawn by other layers for their own steam years. After 1941 the Key System reused the Shattuck, Monterey/Colusa and East Oakland track (Key System layer) and SP kept freight on parts of the 9th Street, Shattuck, 7th Street and Lincoln lines (not drawn, Rule 1).
metadata.mode_note: Tagged interurban (Rule 7): heavy 1,200 V DC electric trains linking separate cities (Berkeley, Albany, Oakland, Alameda, San Leandro) to the ferry and later to San Francisco, often on private right of way. They were run under steam-railroad work rules and could be called commuter_rail; interurban was preferred because they were electric trolley-wire cars, matching how the Key System's parallel transbay trains are treated. The 1912-1926 SP streetcar service is not drawn.
metadata.ownership_note: Rule 4 judgment: all features are Southern Pacific #C1272D, including the 1938-1941 Interurban Electric Railway. IER was incorporated by SP on 14 November 1934; SP kept all 20,000 shares; IER began operating on 1 December 1938, leased SP's facilities for $50,000 a year, ran only the passenger trains (SP kept the steam-hauled freight switching) and kept SP's steam-railroad crew rules (motorman, conductor and flagman). It existed to hold the Bay Bridge franchise and the California Toll Bridge Authority's car-rebuilding money (the TBA took title to 58 cars). Cars were relettered 'Interurban Electric Railway Company' for bridge service, so the trains did carry a distinct name; but with SP-owned stock, SP-leased track, SP rules and a life of under three years, it is treated as SP's operating subsidiary rather than a separate operator. The change is recorded as a 1938 segment boundary in each ferry-era feature and in every bridge-era note. A reviewer who prefers the 'subsidiary running under its own name keeps its own colour' reading (as the Pacific Electric layer does) would split the 1938-1941 segments into IER-coloured features.

segments.note: Electrified successor to the Central Pacific/SP Berkeley Branch steam local (opened 1876-78; steam years are not drawn here - see layer note). Electric service from Oakland Pier up Shattuck Avenue began 23 December 1911; the new extension from Vine Street through the Northbrae Tunnel to Thousand Oaks (Solano and Colusa) opened 1 January 1912, which is why this feature starts in 1912 rather than claiming the last eight days of 1911 for a tunnel section that had only inspection trains. Route: Thousand Oaks - Solano - Northbrae Tunnel - Sutter - Henry - Shattuck (Berkeley station) - Adeline - Stanford - upper level of Oakland 16th Street station - Oakland Pier, where passengers took the SP ferry to the San Francisco Ferry Building. Second-busiest line of the system. The 20-minute headway is the daytime ferry-train frequency the Western Railroader gives for the Oakland and Berkeley lines just before the bridge (40 minutes in the evening); peak-era (c. 1920) service was heavier and is not sourced. Survived the March 1933 SP-Key System consolidation.

segments.note: Bay Bridge era. From 15 January 1939 the Interurban Electric Railway (SP's wholly owned operating subsidiary) ran this line across the lower deck of the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge to the new Transbay Terminal at First and Mission, instead of to a ferry pier. The Berkeley lines turned west at an elevated wye over the SP main line just north of Oakland 16th Street station (the 26th Street flyover) for the Bridge Yard and the bridge; tracks from the Bridge Yard to the terminal were shared with the Key System and Sacramento Northern. Shattuck Avenue was IER Line 3 (local) and Line 9 (express), routed straight to the bridge without calling at 16th Street; the last train of the night ran on from Thousand Oaks over the outer Ninth Street line to Albany. Opening headway 20 minutes daytime / 40 evening; service was cut drastically from 26 February 1940 (new frequency not sourced). Last IER train ran on 25 July 1941 (Western Railroader) or 26 July 1941 (Wikipedia, Northbrae Tunnel article) - SOURCE CONFLICT, both inside 1941. The Key System F line took over the Shattuck track from 6 August 1941. SOURCE CONFLICT on the start: the East Bay Electric Lines article's history section says bridge trains began 'January 1938', its own lead and the Oakland Long Wharf article say January 1939, and the Northbrae Tunnel article says December 1939; the Western Railroader's 15 January 1939 is used (the bridge railway did not open until 1939).
